**Title:** Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists are associated with reduced abdominal aortic aneurysm-related events.

**Authors:** Hyunjun Ahn, David C Kaelber, Nicholas Hoell, Ravi Ambani, Jon G Quatromoni, Ali Khalifeh, Lee Kirksey, Courtney Hanak, Scott J Cameron, Sean P Lyden, Francis J Caputo

**Journal:** Journal of vascular surgery
**Publication Date:** 2026-03-25
**DOI:** 10.1016/j.jvs.2025.11.021
**PMC ID:** 13395541
**Full Text Available:** Yes
**Full Text URL:** https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13395541/


**Abstract:**
Glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have shown to possess cardiovascular protective effects, with preclinical data, suggesting potential benefits in slowing abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) growth. However, their effect on AAA in humans remains underexplored. This study evaluates the effects of GLP-1RAs on all-cause mortality, AAA repair, and acute abdominal aortic syndrome in patients with unruptured AAA.

Glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have shown to possess cardiovascular protective effects, with preclinical data, suggesting potential benefits in slowing abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) growth. However, their effect on AAA in humans remains underexplored. This study evaluates the effects of GLP-1RAs on all-cause mortality, AAA repair, and acute abdominal aortic syndrome in patients with unruptured AAA.

We used the US collaborative network of the TriNetX platform to identify patients aged ≥18 years with unruptured AAA, based on International Classification of Disease, 10th Revision (ICD-10), codes from January 1, 2015, to March 1, 2020. Patients with prior AAA rupture, dissection, repair, and connective tissue disorders were excluded. The remaining cohort was stratified by type 2 diabetes (T2D) status and divided into two cohorts: patients who had GLP-1RA prescription within 6 months before or any time after their first AAA encounter diagnosis during the study period and non-GLP-1RA users who were never prescribed GLP-1RAs. Propensity score matching (1:1) adjusted for demographics, tobacco use, comorbidities, and medications. Five-year odds ratios (ORs) and Kaplan-Meier survival analyses assessed outcomes.

Of the 1407 patients prescribed GLP-1RAs and 38,994 not prescribed GLP-1RAs with T2D, 1401 patients were matched and analyzed. Similarly, among 336 patient prescribed GLP-1RAs and 129,790 not prescribed non-GLP-1RAs without T2D, 336 matched pairs were analyzed. Patient prescribed GLP-1RAs had significantly lower risks of the composite outcome of mortality, AAA repair, and acute abdominal aortic syndrome in both T2D (OR, 0.56; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.47-0.66) and non-T2D cohorts (OR, 0.42; 95% CI, 0.28-0.63). Specifically, those prescribed GLP-1RAs had reduced mortality (T2D: OR, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.45-0.65; non-T2D: OR, 0.47; 95% CI, 0.30-0.74) and were less likely to undergo AAA repair (T2D: OR, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.45-0.95; non-T2D: OR, 0.45; 95% CI, 0.21-0.96). Kaplan-Meier analysis also demonstrated the benefits of GLP-1RAs in delaying outcome.

GLP-1RA prescriptions were associated with a lower risk of clinically important events in patients with unruptured AAA. These findings suggested potential benefits of GLP-1RAs in AAA management, warranting further research on their effect on aneurysm growth and progression.

Keywords: Abdominal aortic aneurysm, Glucagon-like peptide receptor agonists, Aneurysm repair, Aneurysm growth, Medical management

Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), a condition characterized by the weakening and dilation of the abdominal aortic wall, is often discovered incidentally when the rupture risk is low.1,2 The majority of small, asymptomatic AAAs progress to a size requiring endovascular or surgical repair, and there are currently no accepted medical therapies to delay their need for repair.3,4

Although diabetes is a well-recognized risk factor for vascular diseases, observational studies have paradoxically suggested it may be associated with a lower prevalence and slowed progression of AAAs.3,5,6 Several hypotheses have been proposed to explain this relationship, including hyperglycemia-induced stabilization of the extracellular matrix and protective effects of antidiabetic medications.7 Recent evidence has indicated that higher blood glucose levels are positively associated with AAA prevalence among individuals without type 2 diabetes (T2D),8 whereas metformin use—a common diabetes treatment—has been linked to slower AAA growth, supporting the role of antidiabetic pharmacotherapy in modifying AAA risk.9–11

Glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA), initially approved to manage T2D, have demonstrated anti-inflammatory and cardiovascular benefits beyond glycemic control, including heart failure, atrial fibrillation, atherosclerosis, and peripheral artery disease.12–17 Additionally, GLP-1RAs have been shown to inhibit the progression of AAAs in preclinical models,18–21 and active GLP-1 levels have been found to be decreased in a diameter-dependent manner among AAA patients.22 Interestingly, metformin, previously demonstrated to delay AAA growth, was also shown to increase physiological levels of GLP-1.23 Given these properties, it may be reasonable to presume that GLP-1RAs may have therapeutic potential in slowing AAA progression, but their effects on AAA progression remain unexplored. In this study, we aimed to investigate the impact of GLP-1RA prescriptions on the rates of mortality, AAA repair, and other aortic-related outcomes in patients with unruptured AAA, stratified by diabetes status and adjusted for key baseline variables, including demographics, comorbidities, and medications.

This study used the US collaborative network of the TriNetX platform, which includes aggregated and de-identified electronic health records from >120 million adult patients from >60 health care organizations within the United States. Demographic details, diagnoses, procedures, and medications were queried using the International Classification of Diseases Clinical Modification, 10th revision (ICD-10) encounter diagnoses, International Classification of Diseases Procedural Coding System (ICD-10-PCS), RxNorm codes, and Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical codes. This retrospective study is exempt from informed consent. The data are reviewed as a secondary analysis of existing data; this analysis does not involve interventions or interactions with human subjects, and data are deidentified per the deidentification standard defined in Section §164.514(a) of the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) Privacy Rule. Therefore, this study does not qualify as human participant research and does not require institutional review board approval. The process by which the data are deidentified is attested to through a formal determination by a qualified expert as defined in Section §164.514(b) (1) of the HIPAA Privacy Rule. This formal determination by a qualified expert refreshed on December 2020 and was deemed exempt by the MetroHealth Institutional Review Board. The study design and results reporting adhere to the STROBE reporting guidelines.24

The study included patients aged ≥18 years with unruptured AAA (ICD-10 code I71.4) who presented between January 1, 2015, and March 1, 2020. Patients with any ICD-10 encounter diagnoses codes of prior AAA rupture (I71.3), abdominal aortic dissection (I71.02), prior AAA repair (04Q0, 04V0), or connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome (Q87.4) or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (Q79.6) were excluded to focus on degenerative, intact aneurysms.9,10,25 Although GLP-1RAs are commonly prescribed for T2D management, they are increasingly used for weight management. As a result, an exploratory analysis was conducted among patients without T2D by stratifying the study population into T2D and non-T2D groups using ICD-10 encounter diagnosis code E11. These groups were further divided into those never prescribed a GLP-1RA and those prescribed a GLP-1RA, who had at least one GLP-1RA prescription within 6 months before or any time after their initial AAA ICD-10 encounter diagnoses during the study period. RxNorm was used to identify GLP-1RA prescription, which include lixisenatide (1,440,051), albiglutide (1,534,763), duaglutide (1,551,291), semaglutide (1,991,302), liraglutide (475,968), and exenatide (60,548).

All outcomes were analyzed over a 5-year follow-up period, starting at the time of AAA diagnosis and a GLP-1RA prescriptions for GLP-1RA users, and at AAA diagnosis for nonusers. The primary outcome was a composite measure of all-cause mortality, AAA repair (ICD-10-PCS code 04Q0, 04V0), and acute abdominal aortic syndrome (AAAS) defined as either abdominal aortic rupture (ICD-10 code I71.3) or dissection (I71.02).25 Secondary outcomes included each individual component of the primary outcome.

To assess unmeasured confounding, we included several negative control outcomes and negative control exposures.26 We assigned patients with ICD-10 encounter diagnoses of sensorineural hearing loss (H90), viral warts (B07), wrist and hand injury (S62), otitis externa (H60), and sebaceous cyst (L72.3) as a negative control outcome, which are not expected to be different based on GLP-1RA prescriptions. We also assigned ticagrelor (RxNorm code 1116632), immunosuppressants (Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical code L04), and vitamin D supplement (RxNorm code 11253) prescriptions as a negative control exposure, which have been reported to not affect AAA progression.27–29

Before analysis, patient demographics, comorbidities, and laboratory values were adjusted between those prescribed GLP-1RAs and those not prescribed GLP-1RAs using 1:1 propensity score matching with the greedy nearest-neighbor algorithm and a caliper of 0.1 pooled standardized mean difference (SMD). Notably, categorical variables with various cutpoints were created based on historical body mass index and hemoglobin A1c values, because TriNetX does not support the use of these variables as continuous measures during matching. Variables with an SMD of >0.1 after propensity score matching were considered unbalanced.

Statistical significance was set at a P value of <.05 throughout. Continuous variables were reported as mean ± SD and compared using the Student t test, and categorical variables were presented as counts (percentages) and compared using χ2 tests. Odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for all outcomes. Kaplan-Meier survival analyses were conducted and compared using log-rank tests. Patients with outcomes before the inception window were excluded from outcome analysis. All statistical analyses were performed using the native built-in functions of TriNetX, and Kaplan-Meier curves were generated using R version 4.4.2 from the statistical outputs downloaded from TriNetX.

To assess the robustness of our findings, we performed a sensitivity analysis restricted to patients whose recorded encounter diagnosis of unruptured AAA occurred after their initial GLP-1RA prescription among patients with T2D. This analysis could not be performed in patients without T2D owing to the limited sample size. Kaplan-Meier survival analyses were conducted, adjusting for the same covariates using propensity score matching in the main analysis.

Of 185,071 patients with unruptured AAA, 10,629 were excluded owing to the history of AAA repair, rupture, dissection, or connective tissue disorders. Among the remaining 174,442 patients, 43,193 (24.8%) had one or more T2D ICD-10 encounter diagnoses, and 131,249 (75.2%) did not (Fig 1). In the T2D cohort, 38,994 were never prescribed GLP-1RAs (non-GLP-1RA users), 2792 were prescribed GLP-1RAs outside the study period, and 1407 were prescribed GLP-1RAs (GLP-1RA users) during the study period (Fig 1). In the non-T2D cohort, 129,790 were never prescribed GLP-1RAs, 1123 were prescribed GLP-1RAs outside the study period, and 336 were prescribed GLP-1RAs during the study period (Fig 1).

Study flowchart with patient selection criteria. GLP-1RA, glucagon like peptide-1 receptor agonist; T2D, type 2 diabetes.

In the unmatched cohorts, the patients prescribed GLP-1RAs were younger on average (T2D: 68.8 ± 8.7 vs 73.3 ± 9.3 [P < .001]; non-T2D: 68.0 ± 10.2 vs 72.7 ± 10.5 [P < .001]) and had a higher proportion of males (T2D: 71.6% vs 67.3% [P = .001]; non-T2D: 76.8% vs 67.2% [P < .001]) (Tables I and II). GLP-1RA users in the T2D cohort were more likely to be White (76.4% vs 71.1%; P < .001), whereas no significant differences were observed in the non-T2D cohort (Tables I and II). In both the T2D and non-T2D cohorts, GLP-1RA users had a higher prevalence of comorbidities, greater medication use, and higher body mass index levels compared with nonusers (Tables I and II). After propensity score matching, 1401 patients with T2D and 336 patients without T2D remained in each cohort (Fig 1). A balance of covariates was achieved across all variables except for the proportion of patients diagnosed with liver disease in the non-T2D cohorts, with a greater prevalence of liver disease observed among patients prescribed GLP-1RAs (Tables I and II). Summaries of baseline characteristics and SMDs for all covariates before and after matching are provided in Tables I and II for each cohort.

Among patients with T2D, patients prescribed GLP-1RAs had a significantly lower rate of the composite outcome of all-cause mortality, aneurysm repair, and AAAS compared with those not prescribed GLP-1RAs (OR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.47-0.66) (Fig 2). Specifically, GLP-1RA users had lower rates of all-cause mortality (OR, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.45-0.65) and aneurysm repair (OR, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.45-0.95). No significant difference was observed in AAAS (OR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.60-1.60). Kaplan-Meier survival analysis further demonstrated a delay in composite outcomes (HR 0.59; 95% CI, 0.51-0.68) and aneurysm repair (HR 0.63; 95% CI, 0.43-0.90) among patient prescribed GLP-1RAs (Fig 3, A, and B).

In the non-T2D cohort, GLP-1RA prescriptions were associated with a significantly lower rate of the composite outcome (OR, 0.42; 95% CI, 0.28-0.63). Specifically, GLP-1RA prescriptions decreased all-cause mortality (OR, 0.47; 95% CI, 0.30-0.74) and aneurysm repair (OR, 0.45; 95% CI, 0.21-0.96) (Fig 2). Kaplan-Meier survival analysis further demonstrated a delay in composite outcomes (HR 0.47; 95% CI, 0.32-0.68) and aneurysm repair (HR 0.32; 95% CI, 0.14-0.75) among those prescribed GLP-1RAs (Fig 3, C and D).

Our study revealed no significant differences in the OR of negative control outcomes, including sensorineural hearing loss, viral warts, wrist and hand injuries, otitis externa, and sebaceous cysts, between those prescribed GLP-1RA and those not prescribed GLP-1RAs in T2D cohort (Supplementary Fig 1, online only). Among the non-T2D cohort, a negative control outcome analysis was only feasible for sensorineural hearing loss because the low number of events for other outcomes could not be analyzed as TriNetX obscures any count of <10 by reporting it as 10 to protect patient health information. No significant differences in the OR of sensorineural hearing loss was noted in non-T2D cohort.

Risks of AAA repair also showed no significant difference when ticagrelor, immunosuppressants, and vitamin D supplement prescriptions were introduced as negative control exposures among both the T2D and non-T2D cohort (Supplementary Fig 2, online only).

A total of 1092 patients with T2D who had at least one GLP-1RA prescription before their AAA encounter diagnosis during the study period were matched and analyzed in the sensitivity analysis. The sensitivity analysis demonstrated a lower risk of aneurysm repair over the 5-year follow-up period in the T2D cohort (Supplementary Fig 3, online only). Additionally, no significant differences in AAA repair risk were observed when ticagrelor, immunosuppressants, and vitamin D supplements were introduced as negative control exposures in the sensitivity analysis (Supplementary Fig 3, online only).

Prior studies have demonstrated that GLP-1RAs provide cardiovascular protective effects beyond glycemic control, but their impact on AAA outcomes has remained unexplored.1215 To the best of our knowledge, this clinical study is the first to evaluate the effects of GLP-1RAs on AAA-related outcomes. Using robust propensity score matching, we found that GLP-1RA prescriptions were associated with a significant decrease in the rates of clinically meaningful events among patients with AAA, including a delay in AAA repair, regardless of diabetes status.

In our study population, the majority of patients with AAAs were male and White, consistent with prior findings.30 Furthermore, aligning with the previously described paradoxical relationship between diabetes and AAA prevalence, our study found a greater prevalence of unruptured AAAs among patients without T2D.6,7 Prior studies have consistently observed that metformin use is associated with slower AAA enlargement among patients with T2D.9,10 We demonstrated here that GLP-1RA prescriptions were also associated with a lower risk of AAA-related outcomes, even after adjusting for baseline metformin prescriptions. This finding suggests that GLP-1RAs may provide additional vascular protective effects in AAAs beyond those attributed to metformin. Although the precise mechanisms underlying metformin’s effect on AAA is multifaceted and unclear, it has been reported to upregulate physiological GLP-1 levels, raising the possibility that direct GLP-1RA administration may confer more targeted vascular benefits.23

The results of the present study build on several preclinical studies that have shown that GLP-1RAs may prevent endothelial dysfunction and provide vascular protective effects in AAA.18–21 The pathogenesis of AAA is thought to be largely driven by oxidative stress and inflammation, marked by macrophage and lymphocyte infiltration, which triggers the release of proinflammatory cytokines and activation of matrix metalloproteinases, leading to the degradation of the extracellular matrix.31,32 Several experimental mouse models have demonstrated that GLP-1RAs can attenuate these pathological processes through their anti-inflammatory and antioxidant mechanisms, including suppression of reactive oxygen species production, reduction of proinflammatory cytokines, and inhibition of matrix metalloproteinase activity, thereby modifying the risk of AAA formation and progression.18–21 Inhibition of these multifactorial pathogenic mechanisms may account for our observation that patients prescribed GLP-1 RAs in this study exhibited a lower incidence and delayed onset of clinically significant events.

The present findings, in conjunction with supporting preclinical evidence, suggest that GLP-1RAs may mitigate the progression of and risk associated with AAA, offering novel insight into their potential protective role in patients with AAA. Given the expanding use of GLP-1RAs for weight management and cardiovascular protection, our results underscore the possibility of the broader therapeutic utility for GLP-1RAs beyond their traditional metabolic indications.33,34 Nonetheless, although our analysis leveraged data from a large, multicenter network of health care organizations, it remains exploratory. Further research is warranted to validate these observational findings, including studies that directly assess changes in aneurysm diameter over time and whether GLP-1RAs can also prevent AAA formation.

This study has several important limitations to consider. First, its observational nature limits causal inference and may include residual confounding despite robust propensity score matching. It is possible that patients prescribed GLP-1RAs could have had greater health awareness and undertaken lifestyle modification with improved weight management, which could have independently improve outcomes. Second, the absence of discrete radiological imaging information in TriNetX precluded direct assessment of AAA size progression. However, the use of AAA repair may provide a clinically meaningful surrogate of disease progression, and our negative control exposure analyses, which demonstrated no significant differences in AAA repair rates, suggest the validity of the measure. Third, the aggregate nature of the data limited the ability to investigate individual patient cases, precluding detailed assessments of GLP-1RA dosage, adherence, duration of use, lifestyle interventions, and duration of diabetes. Similarly, because TriNetX does not provide the identities or geographical location of the participating health care organizations or information on their respective data contributions, potential heterogeneity at the hospital could not be accounted for. Mortality data may also be subject to reporting delays from some health care organizations, because many patients die outside of a hospital or emergency department.35 However, prior studies have reported lower mortality rates among GLP-1RA users, and, if confirmed, the protective effects of GLP-1RAs in AAA patients could have substantial public health implications.36,37 Furthermore, the inability to perform competing risk analyses, because the platform does not support traditional methods such as Fine-Gray models, may have limited accurate modeling of competing events. We acknowledge this as an important consideration and propose that future investigations incorporate methodologies capable of accounting for competing risks to further validate our findings.

It should also be noted that, for GLP-1RA users, the index date was defined as the later of either the AAA diagnosis or the initiation of GLP-1RA prescription in the main analysis. This approach was designed to minimize the exclusion of patients with unruptured AAA while ensuring that only 5-year outcomes occurring after initial medication exposure were captured. Although this definition may have introduced potential immortal-time bias, both the negative control exposure analysis and the sensitivity analysis suggest that it did not significantly affect the results. Nevertheless, caution is warranted when interpreting findings among non-T2D patients, because a sensitivity analysis could not be performed owing to the limited sample size. Last, reliance on ICD-10 encounter diagnosis codes introduces the potential for misclassification bias, which may lead to the under-reporting of AAA events.35,38
40 Nevertheless, it is worth noting that any misclassification would likely to affect both groups nondifferentially, and the observed differences between GLP-1RA users and nonusers remained significant, suggesting the association may be robust despite potential underestimation. Furthermore, the absence of significant associations in the negative control outcomes and exposure analyses suggests minimal information bias and strengthens the reliability of our findings.

Our study, using data from a large network of health care organizations, found that GLP-1RA prescriptions were associated with a significant decrease in clinically important events, including the delay in the need for AAA repair, over a 5-year follow-up. Despite these encouraging outcomes, the findings should be interpreted as hypothesis generating owing to the limited granularity inherent to large database research. Further investigations are warranted to validate these associations and to evaluate the efficacy in slowing AAA progression. Nevertheless, our study represents an important initial step toward understanding the potential role of GLP-1RAs in the management of patients with AAA.

Type of Research: Multicenter, retrospective, propensity score-matched study

Key Findings: Among 1401 matched patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and 336 matched patients without T2D with unruptured abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAAs), glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist prescriptions were associated with lower rates of mortality (T2D: odds ratio [OR], 0.54; 95% CI, 0.45-0.65; non-T2D: OR, 0.47; 95% CI, 0.30-0.74) and AAA repair (T2D: OR, 0.66, 0.45-0.95; non-T2D: OR, 0.45; 95% CI, 0.21-0.96) over a 5-year follow-up period.

Take Home Message: These findings suggest the potential benefits of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists in AAA management, warranting further investigations to confirm these associations.
